title: Vertigo: Dix–Hallpike and Epley
stem: Cubicle 25. Mrs Chau, 58, has had brief spells of spinning (under a minute) when she rolls over in bed or looks up, for 3 days. She is well between spells. Perform the appropriate positional test and treatment on her.

phases.title: Choose the test
phases.goal: Which test for this pattern, and is it safe?

phases.title: Dix–Hallpike
phases.goal: Do it properly and read the eyes.

phases.title: Epley
phases.goal: Treat the side that is positive.

notes:
Checked against the AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline on BPPV (2017), and emergency approaches to the dizzy patient (TiTrATE, HINTS; Kattah 2009).

Choose the test by the pattern: brief positional (triggered) episodes with no vertigo at rest → Dix–Hallpike for BPPV; continuous acute vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus (acute vestibular syndrome) → HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew), done by a trained examiner; do not use the Dix–Hallpike in acute vestibular syndrome and do not use HINTS in episodic positional vertigo (your notes make this point well).

Dix–Hallpike: explain, warn about vertigo, sit with legs out so the head will hang over the end, turn the head 45° to one side, lie back quickly with the neck extended ~20° below horizontal, hold at least 30 seconds, watch for torsional upbeating nystagmus (latency a few seconds, lasts under a minute, fatigues), sit up. Positive → Epley on that side (turn the head 90° to the other side, then roll onto the side with the nose down, then sit up), each held about 30 seconds. Central features: no latency, persistent, direction-changing or vertical downbeat nystagmus without torsion, other neurology.

Your notes match (including Epley and the central/peripheral table). Contraindications to positional testing: severe neck disease, carotid disease, vertebral dissection risk.

steps.hint: Brief positional episodes, well between: Dix–Hallpike, not HINTS.
